analysis: The broad option covers media forms, cultural memory, representation, textual analysis and production through the media courses, literature, sociology and rhetoric. Documentary and rhetorical work apply analysis to production and public communication. Psychology supplies audience context, and qualitative methods and historical research support inquiry. These complementary courses do not substitute for a dedicated media methods sequence.

The industries option keeps media analysis and documentary work while giving greater weight to marketing, consumer behaviour, market evidence, international business and organisational strategy. Those courses supply tools for studying media markets and audiences. They do not claim sector-specific training in media careers or journalism.

The digital option couples media history and representation with programming, data management, statistics, machine learning and the ethics of AI. Digital strategy and consumer engagement add organisational and audience dimensions. Computing courses provide methods and conceptual context, not a platform design or journalism sequence.

The options remain distinctly organised and have feasible 180 EC schedules. Journalism and political participation remain evidenced directions beyond the three-option limit. Research seminar, advanced methods, professional writing, content creation and the thesis remain separate where the correspondence is too broad.
constructionStop: Three coherent, distinct options reach the programme limit.
